To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

androgen receptor‐mediated transcription and signaling are the major drivers of prostate cancer cell growth and survival, and that the steroidogenic pathway is an attractive target for therapeutic intervention.

1) the AR is a key player in the development of hormone‐naive and CRPC, and 2) the steroidogenic pathway is an alternative source of androgen that can be used to maintain androgen receptor activity in prostate cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (i) the molecular changes that occur in the androgen receptor (AR) and its co‐regulators during the transition of prostate cancer from androgen‐dependent to CRPC; (ii) the molecular changes in the steroidogenic pathways that occur during the same transition; and (iii) the molecular changes of AR‐independent signalling pathways in the same transition.
the mechanisms that prostate cancers use to escape androgen‐deprivation therapy (ADT).
the identification of the mechanisms that allow prostate cancer cells to survive in an androgen‐depleted environment, and to become resistant to hormonal treatments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the androgen receptor (AR) is the main target in the treatment of CRPC, and that AR signalling pathways are the most important pathways to be targeted.
prostate cancer cells have multiple mechanisms that allow them to escape the antiandrogenic effect of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).
androgen deprivation does not completely eradicate the androgen receptor, and that the androgen receptor is not the only driver in prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the androgen receptor (AR) is a key player in prostate carcinogenesis, and that its activity is maintained during the development of castration‐resistance.
androgen deprivation is only the start of a series of molecular and cellular events that ultimately leads to the development of CRPC.

the prostate cancer cell is a master of survival, and it will use all possible mechanisms to survive and proliferate, even when androgen levels are reduced to a level that would normally be considered as castrated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the androgen receptor (AR) is a master regulator of the prostate, and it is not surprising that the AR is a major target for prostate cancer.
androgen‐dependent prostate cancer cells have a number of ways to survive androgen deprivation.
prostate cancer cells can adapt to castration‐mediated androgen depletion by using alternative pathways that can maintain intratumoural androgens.
